participants: Chris Klevan (sales manager, running the meeting)
Kim Forbes-Sobers (setter; referred to throughout as 'he' and 'brother')
summary: A 61-minute Monday sales meeting covering wins, last week's numbers rep by rep, projection rebalancing, marketing questions and a live call review. Chris opens with wins, then takes Andrew, Richard, Michael and Kim through last week's performance, teaching a standard reporting format he wants used going forward: slots booked, calls shown, closes, deposits, and the most common objection. Each rep then redistributes their shortfall into later weeks of the month on a shared projection sheet. Richard asks about ad strategy and about a publicly advertised $200/month price that is anchoring prospects before they reach a $6,000 call. The final ten minutes are a group review of Andrew's closed call with Dan Keogh, in which the manager critiques Andrew for jumping to payment-plan options instead of running the open-wallet sequence, and then delivers an extended rationale for advising prospects to put the $6,000 on a credit card. Richard voices discomfort with that advice and is talked through it. The meeting ends with the manager's 'let it go' detachment framing and a joke about calling prospects.
notable: PROSPECTS ARE ROUTINELY IDENTIFIED BY SEXUAL ORIENTATION AND ETHNICITY, by both reps and the manager, throughout the meeting and unchallenged by anyone. Andrew: 'Tom, yeah, the gay one'; 'Because I pressured the gay guy'; 'Eddie, the Asian guy'; 'the Dutch guy'. Chris, adopting the same frame: 'so did you pressure all three of the gay guys? Is that what you're saying?' The meeting's closing line, from Andrew: 'All right, let's... Call up some gay guys', to which Chris replies 'Any guys.' This sits alongside the nationality-based disqualification instruction recorded in the 06/30 one-to-one and should be read as one pattern, not two incidents.

CREDIT CARD ADVICE IS EXPLICIT MANAGER POLICY. Chris, teaching the open wallet: 'when you find out they have the cash, you're like, okay, dude, like, can I tell you what I would do if I were you? Yeah, I would pay all from I would do the whole thing. I'd put it on that credit card.' He gives a full rationale — 'if you're investing $6,000 now on a credit card that will give you the flexibility to pay it off over the next two or three years... you're not going to be thinking about it in three or four years' — and adds a hypothetical about a prospect with '$20,000 available' at '0% interest for the next 15 months'. He closes with the only caveat: 'But it isn't the best move for everyone. It isn't, it definitely isn't.'

A REP RAISED AN ETHICAL OBJECTION TO THE CREDIT CARD ADVICE AND WAS COACHED PAST IT. Richard: 'That's I do need to learn. Like, understand the whole doing the open wallet, but then advising someone and putting it on a credit card. And maybe it's because I haven't grown up with credit cards. Like, I've always been taught, like, you need to be able to pay it off, like, without a credit card. But that's something that's something I need to work on myself, too.' The concern is reframed as the rep's own limiting belief rather than examined.

THE CLOSE REVIEWED AS EXEMPLARY WAS FUNDED ON CREDIT BY AN ILLIQUID BUYER. Andrew describing the Dan Keogh close: 'he bought a house in California, cash. So he got flushed out of cash, but he said he's taking another job, and we went through the open wallet, and then I figured out, okay, like, he could do six times 1,200, but I figured out, hey, like, he told me his credit score was 700-something. I was like, dude, put it on a credit card, and I figured out, yeah, PayVide is going to be the best solution.' In the recording played back, the prospect states he spent $300,000 cash on a house, has no cash, has taken a second job earning about $2,400 extra of which half goes to his mortgage. Michael called it 'a really phenomenal call' and Chris said 'That's it, baby.'

A DEPOSIT WAS TAKEN FROM A PROSPECT WITH A NEGATIVE BANK BALANCE AND REPORTED AS A GOOD OUTCOME. Richard: 'I had, uh, one person just didn't have any money. Dick had two deposits, even one from a guy that had minus six. 67 bucks in his account when I had to call with him, so I feel like I did okay with that lead.' No one questioned it.

DEPOSITS ARE COUNTED AS CLOSES IN THE REPORTED CLOSE RATE. Chris to Richard: 'so you had 2 deposits, 1 unit, so that's technically 3 people that committed... so then you close 3 out of 9, so that's 33%, essentially.' Richard confirms none have converted — 'No, they're not in yet.' This is the second corpus instance of deposits being counted as units, after the 06/30 one-to-one where 13 closes became 14 'in a deposit'.

A DEPOSIT KNOWN TO BE HOLLOW REMAINED IN THE NUMBERS. Andrew overheard a prospect after the Zoom ended because a parallel phone line stayed open: 'I heard him talking with his wife, so, oh yeah, I had to pay this guy, but I don't think he will [buy]. He just made me a courtesy.' Chris: 'Yeah, sometimes people will do that.' Andrew also holds a separate $100 deposit from a prospect who 'got scared'; Chris instructs returning it, with the reason given as chargeback risk: 'if they get super scared and they don't want to get on the phone with you again, then they might just charge it back. You don't want to do that.'

AN AUTOMATED AGENT NAMED 'SOPHIA' CONTACTS PROSPECTS AND IS SPOKEN OF AS A PERSON. Chris: 'SalesKick was a bit wonky. Sophia was going rogue, doing some really weird stuff. Wouldn't be surprised if a lot of people were a little bit upset about that.' He instructs closers to work around her and to disclose the automation if pressed: 'if Sophia is acting a fool, then just make it, just take accountability and be like, look, I know that the bot is kind of on the fritz a little bit.' Cross-reference: the prospect Eddie on 07/03 said 'I got a text message from a girl saying that I have a meeting with you', and Kim, the human setter, is referred to as male throughout this meeting.

A PUBLICLY ADVERTISED $200/MONTH PRICE IS ANCHORING PROSPECTS AND THE FIX IS DEPRIORITISED. Richard: 'The 200 a month. I had someone today and he read that online, so that's exactly what he expected... he said like, yeah, I wouldn't have booked a meeting if it was six grand because I just can't do that right now.' Chris: 'No, that's for Primal University... It's a lower priority because all of our focus is on marketing right now... it's not ideal when somebody. Everybody comes in with a price anchor like that.' The instruction is to downsell those prospects into Primal University instead.

A REP SELF-REPORTS PRESSURING PROSPECTS AND THE MANAGER OBJECTS TO THE WORD, NOT THE BEHAVIOUR. Andrew: 'I didn't close the ones that I should have closed... Because I pressured the gay guy' and later 'he didn't feel, after that conversation, like, pressured, like, my people.' Chris: 'I don't like that word, pressure.' Andrew on another prospect: 'I could have pressured him a little bit more, maybe.'

A REP WHO SELF-ASSESSED AS NOT READY WAS KEPT ON CALLS BECAUSE HE CLOSED ONE. Michael: 'I probably should have taken a bit more time before hopping on calls, to be honest.' Chris: 'You took calls. You got a PIF. You wouldn't have had the PIF otherwise. It all happens how it's supposed to.'

THE $7,200 INSTALMENT STRUCTURE IS CONFIRMED AS ROUTINE. Andrew: 'he could do six times 1,200'; and in the played-back recording, 'We can do the six months, but it's going to be, like, 1,200...' Six payments of $1,200 totals $7,200 against a $6,000 stated price. The prospect in the recording had asked 'is there any way I can make less payments on that time, like every month' and was told 'it's like another $1,000.'

THIRD-PARTY CONSUMER FINANCING IS IN ACTIVE USE AND FAILING. Referred to variously as PayVide, Paiva and Pivot, plus PayPal Credit as a fallback. Two declines in one weekend, attributed to a student applicant and to a $2,000 credit limit where 'you only got approved for 1,000, but of course not for six.' Chris: 'We're working on a couple of different financing partners.'

MARKETING STATE: ads run only to warm retargeting traffic, no cold traffic yet; Instagram output moving from one post a day to 30 pieces per week; messaging shifting to explicitly sell coaching; a VSL is written and about to be shot.

PROJECTIONS ARE REBALANCED RATHER THAN MISSED. Each rep moves their shortfall into later weeks on a live shared sheet — Andrew redistributing $14,800, Richard $10,000, Michael $2,000 and a unit. Chris confirms recurring payments do not count toward the target: 'Nope. This is just new cash.' Andrew is 'pacing like 81' against a $100,000 July projection.

Reported weekly numbers: Andrew two closes on the day of the meeting including a follow-up recovery, roughly $12,000; Richard nine live calls, one unit, two deposits, two FDQs; Michael eight calls, one close, three finance blockers; Kim five sets against six, one unit, with weekend pickup rate cited as the cause.

Reps are reviewing each other's recorded prospect calls as training material — Michael watched Andrew's calls, Andrew watched Michael's 'call with the surfer guy' several times and transcribed the objection handling 'word to word'. Relevant to how prospect recordings are used and retained.
No recording disclosure or consent appears anywhere in the transcript, on a call that discusses named prospects, their finances and their credit scores.
